claims.text: High dislocation density in Q235 steel promotes formation of a uniform and adherent Fe-oxide passive film.
Dislocations act as active nucleation sites for oxidation and passivation-film formation.
Grain boundaries provide additional nucleation sites for oxidation in the passivation layer.
A continuous and adherent passive film minimizes localized anodic-cathodic differences.
Minimizing localized anodic-cathodic differences suppresses localized corrosion.
Low-temperature annealing at 300°C for 2 hours reduces the dislocation density of Q235 steel.
Annealing at 300°C for 2 hours can reduce dislocation density while causing only minimal change in grain size.
Lower dislocation density provides fewer oxidation nucleation sites.
Lower dislocation density produces a discontinuous, heterogeneous, and less protective oxide film.
The less protective film associated with lower dislocation density increases corrosion rates in harsh environments.
Elevated temperature enhances diffusion kinetics and makes the low-dislocation-density material particularly susceptible to localized corrosion.
Cold-worked Q235 specimens will form a more uniform and protective oxide layer than annealed Q235 specimens.
Cold-worked Q235 specimens will exhibit lower corrosion current, pitting density, and mass loss than annealed specimens.
The untreated, as-received Q235 steel is a cold-worked, high-dislocation-density state.
Maintaining grain size between the treatment groups isolates dislocation density as the primary experimental variable.
Thermal treatment may cause grain growth or segregation that independently affects corrosion behavior.

Statistically indistinguishable oxide-film morphology and corrosion performance between the cold-worked and annealed groups at both temperatures would refute the proposed dominant role of dislocation density.
